parties:
Musa Ali ------- Appellant
Vs.
Nur Ahmed and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
6. The contesting defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4, heirs of original tenant Abdul Hakim and others, contended in their joint written statement that there was never any auction-sale of the suit land and Badruddoza never obtained possession of the suit land. Abdul Hakim and others never left for Arakan. The alleged pattadars from Badruddoza never possessed the suitland on the basis of any patta. As such by purchase from some of them, the plaintiff also did not acquire any right, title and interest in the suit land and the contesting defendants never threatened him with dispossession. These defendants have been possessing the suit land from the time of their ancestors. The suit land has been recorded in the S.A. Khatian in their names. They have sold 2 kanis of land to one Kabir Ahmed Master. Yusuf Ali, an alleged pattadar, filed a criminal case against the defendants in respect of the suit, but he lost. 

 8. The lower appellate Court also found that there was no sale certificate and and writ of delivery of possession and that Ext.8 did not show any particulars so as to connect it with the suit land. The rate of rent of the suit khatian also did not tally with the total claim of 4 year's rent as in Ext. 8. Yet the lower appellate Court held that the suit land was attracted by Ext. 8, because "it was not the case of the defendants that Abdul Hakim and others held any other land in their tenancy under Badruddoza Chowdhury." It further held that there was no documentary evidence to show that the tenants gave up their possession of the suit holding in favour of the landlord on gelling exemption from payment of balance decretal dues. But the subsequent conduct of the landlord, namely, the settlement with proforma-defendant Nos. 21-30 stand proved by the pattas Ext.5 series, Touzi Ext.3 series and Bakijai Ext.4 series, which are in the handwriting of Badruddoza Chowdhury. The lower appellate Court held that from the evidence of the plaintiff as PWI "nothing satisfactory regarding the possession of his vendors could be found". It also found that the story of Abdul Hakim and others leaving for Arakan was inconsistent. As regards the pattadar's possession, the lower appellate Court relied upon the evidence of P.Ws. 3,4 and 5, and on a consideration of Exts. 3, 4, C(2) to C(4) and Ext. G, found that the pattas were acted upon and that the pattadars possessed the suit land till they were dispossessed by the contesting defendants in 1956. The suit having been filed in 1958, it was not barred by limitation. Hence the trial Court's judgment and decree were set aside and the suit was decreed. 

 10. Leave was granted to consider whether in the absence of sale certificate, writ of delivery of possession and particulars to connect the suit land with the suit Register Ext. 8, the auction-sale was established by evidence. Leave was also granted to consider whether in view of the facts that as heirs of the original tenant the defendants' names were recorded in the RS and SA khatians, that the revenue authorities found the contesting defendants to be in possession of the suit land upon objections being raised by the plaintiffs vendors, that the criminal Courts too found possession of the contesting defendants in the suit land, it was imperative upon the lower appellate Court to decide the question of limitation from the standpoint as to whether the plaintiff filed the suit within 12 years of dispossession. The two Courts below concurrently found that the contesting defendants got their homestead in the suit land, a fact which belies the plaintiffs claim that Abdul Hakim and others had voluntarily surrendered possession of the suit land to the landlord and left for Arakan and leave was granted also to consider whether the story of voluntary surrender of possession was established by evidence. 

 16. Both the Courts below concurrently found from copies of orders in criminal cases and revenue proceedings, Ext. C series that the contesting defendants were in possession of the suit land. But the two Courts differed with regard to the period of possession. The trial Court noticed the report of the Revenue Circle Officer on local inquiry stating that the heirs of Abdul Hakim and others were in possession of lands of suit holding all along since RS operation (in 1940 or 1941, i.e. a few years after the pattadars allegedly went into possession). The lower appellate Court did not consider the RS record at all, which stands in the name of the contesting defendants, but considered only the SA khatian Ext. D and held that the defendants came to possess the suit land since 1956. The lower appellate Court has not explained why this particular year was selected for the purpose of this finding. No. averment in the plaint has been referred to, no evidence either. This finding seems to be a gratuitous finding in favour of the plaintiff. The lowest common denominator in the judgments of the two Courts below is that the plaintiffs vendors were out of possession in 1956. When the plaintiff purchased the suit land in 1958 he never obtained possession. When he filed the suit in 1958 he and his vendors were already out of possession. The case is squarely covered by Article 142 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act. The trial Court holds that the suit is barred by limitation, because the defendants are in possession since the time of their ancestors. The lower appellate Court holds that the suit in not barred by limitation because the plaintiffs vendors were dispossessed in 1956, which is neither the plaintiffs case nor the defendants, and which is clearly based on conjecture and surmise, not on evidence on record. The plaintiff, having been concurrently found to be out of possession at the time of the institution of the suit was required to allege in the plaint and prove at the trial that he and his vendors were dispossessed within 12 years before the institution of the suit. He has failed to do either. The suit is thus barred by limitation. The lower appellate Court and the High Court Division failed to decide the issue in its correct perspective. 

 21. Plaintiff filed a suit for declaration of title, confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of khas possession in the suit land and also for permanent injunction. Plaintiffs case, in short, is that, the suit land belonged to Abdul Hakim and others in raiyati interest under landlord Badruddoza Chowdhury predecessors-in-interest of proforma-defendants 31-34 as recorded in RS. khatian. The landlord obtained a decree in Rent Suit No. 780 of 1934 against the tenants and in Rent Execution Case No. 721 of 1935 auction purchased the holding for Rs. 25/- after exempting the balance of the decretal dues as the tenants were unable to pay the balance of Tk.129/- and odd. In such circumstances, the tenants gave up possession amicably in favour of landlord Badaraddoza Chowdhury who held the land for two years in khas possession after merging the raiyati with his Taluki interest. Abdul Hakim and others were entangled in a murder case and they were sentenced to jail and after release from jail they left for Arakan and other places. The landlord settled 5 kanis of lands out of entire 6 kanis of the holding toproforma defendants 21-30 on 26.1.1937 by pattas and the rest one kani is in possession of the heirs of Badaraddoza namely, proforma defendants 31-34. Plaintiff purchased the suitland of Schedule 11 of the plaint out of the land of Schedule I from proforma defendants 21, 22, 28 and 29 by kahala on 30.5. 1958 and is in possession of the same. According to the plaintiff, Abdul Hakim, others and their heirs defendants have no title and possession in the suit land. The positive case of the plaintiff, is that, defendant No. 17, a pleader's clerk who conducted the suit at his instance the defendants threatened the plaintiff with dispossession as defendant No. 17 failed to purchase the land. 

 "Seeing these defects, I think, in the plaint a story had been introduced that the tenant Abdul Hakim and others amicably gave up possession of suit lands of Khatian 252 and obtained remission of the balance of the decretal dues as the landlord auction purchased the land for Rs. 25.00 only."
